title: Moko Jumbie: The Tall Guardian
summary: On the night before a village festival, a young stilt-walker named Corwin learns why the Moko Jumbie towers above the rooftops — not for spectacle, but to see the spirits that creep toward the sleeping village.
full_text:
The festival of Notting Hill was still a week away, but in the village of Chateaubelair the preparations had already begun. Corwin Baptiste, who was sixteen and lanky as a breadfruit sapling, had been chosen to walk on stilts for the first time. His uncle, Master Raymond, was the village's oldest Moko Jumbie, and he had spent three evenings teaching Corwin to balance on bamboo poles that raised him seven feet above the earth.

'You think this is about dancing,' Master Raymond said, wiping clay from his hands. 'It is not about dancing. The height is the point. When you are up there, you see what others cannot. You see what comes.'

Corwin did not understand. He thought the stilts were tradition, a spectacle, something tourists photographed and children cheered. He had never considered that the towering figure might serve a purpose beyond carnival.

The night before the festival, a storm rolled in from the Atlantic — not a proper hurricane, but a thick, wet darkness that pressed against the windows and made the candles gutter. Corwin lay in his hammock listening to the wind rattle the zinc roof when he heard a sound that did not belong to the storm. It was a low, rhythmic tapping, like a walking stick on packed earth, and it was coming from the road.

He rose and went to the window. The moon had broken through the clouds, and in its pale light he saw a figure moving down the road on stilts. It was impossibly tall — taller than any man on poles had a right to be — and it moved with a slow, deliberate gait that shook the ground with each step. The figure wore a headdress of shells and raffia that clicked and whispered in the wind, and its body was draped in layers of cloth that caught the moonlight and threw it back in fragments.

Corwin knew what it was. Every child in Saint Vincent knew. The Moko Jumbie.

But this was not Master Raymond. This was something older, something that had walked these roads long before the village existed. The figure stopped beneath Corwin's window and turned its head — if a mask could turn — and looked directly at him. He felt the gaze like a hand pressed to his chest.

Then the Moko Jumbie lifted one stilt and pointed down the road, toward the cluster of houses where families slept. Corwin followed the gesture and saw, or thought he saw, a shadow moving between the houses. It was not the shadow of a cloud or a tree. It moved against the wind, low to the ground, and where it passed, the dogs whimpered and went silent.

The Moko Jumbie began to walk toward it. Each step was slow and enormous, and with every stride the shell headdress rang like a bell. The shadow froze, then recoiled. It gathered itself and fled toward the sea, dissolving into the darkness like smoke into water.

The Moko Jumbie stood at the edge of the village and watched it go. Then it turned back, looked once more at Corwin, and walked — walked upward, as though the air were solid — until it was gone.

In the morning, Corwin told Master Raymond what he had seen. The old man nodded slowly and handed him the stilts.

'Now you understand,' he said. 'The Moko Jumbie does not walk for the crowd. The Moko Jumbie walks for the village. The height is not pride. It is vigilance. You see evil before it arrives, and you stand tall enough that it knows it has been seen.'

That afternoon, Corwin walked on stilts for the festival, and the crowd cheered and the music played. But his eyes were not on the dancers below. They were on the rooftops, the roads, the spaces between houses where shadows pooled. He walked tall, and he watched, and he understood at last what the old tradition meant — that the tallest figure in the village was not a performer but a sentinel, a guardian raised above the world so that no harm could approach unseen.
moral: True guardianship is not spectacle but vigilance — to stand above the crowd is to see what the crowd cannot, and to bear that sight is a sacred responsibility.

title: Rounces: The Night Riders
summary: A fisherman who mocks his grandmother's warnings about the Rounces discovers that the spirit-animals which ride the sleeping have their own terrible logic, and that the paralysis they bring is not cruelty but a test of the soul.
full_text:
Old Celia Baptiste had rules about sleep. She told her grandchildren every time they stayed at her house in Georgetown: do not sleep on your back, do not sleep with your feet pointing toward the door, and if you wake and cannot move, do not fight. Let it pass. Say nothing. Breathe.

Her grandson Derek, who was fourteen and thought his grandmother superstitious, broke all three rules on the same night.

It happened during the mango season, when the air was so thick with the sweetness of overripe fruit that even breathing felt like eating. Derek had eaten too much, slept too late, and fallen asleep on his back with his feet toward the door because the room was small and the hammock swung that way. He dreamed of nothing at all, and then he was awake — or believed he was.

He could not move. His arms were at his sides, his legs straight, his head turned slightly to the left. He could see the room: the candle guttering on the shelf, the gecko frozen on the wall, the moonlight coming through the window in a blade. He could hear the tree frogs and the distant thump of a bass drum from some party in the hills. But he could not lift a finger or turn his head or make any sound at all.

Then he felt the weight. It began at his chest — a pressure, heavy and warm, as though something large had settled onto him. It was not painful, but it was absolute, and it was alive. He could feel it breathing, or perhaps it was his own breathing slowed and deepened until each inhale was a labour and each exhale a relief.

In the corner of his vision, something moved. It was not a person and not quite an animal. It was a shape, dark and indistinct, with the suggestion of limbs and the certainty of presence. It did not approach him. It sat in the corner of the room, watching, and its watching was a weight in itself.

Derek tried to fight. He strained against the paralysis with every muscle, and for his effort the weight on his chest doubled. He could not breathe. The room dimmed. The shape in the corner leaned forward, and he felt something that was not quite fear and not quite understanding — a recognition that this was not punishment but something older and more impersonal, like weather.

He stopped fighting. He let the weight settle. He breathed as his grandmother had instructed — slowly, deeply, without thought. The pressure eased. The shape in the corner sat back. Time passed in a way that had nothing to do with clocks.

When morning came, Derek was on his side, facing the wall, and the room was empty and bright. He lay there for a long time, listening to the roosters and the sea. Then he went to his grandmother and told her everything.

Old Celia nodded. 'The Rounces ride those who sleep with their doors open,' she said. 'They are not evil. They test. They press the chest to see if the spirit is strong enough to bear weight. You fought, and it nearly crushed you. You yielded, and it passed.'

'What are they?' Derek asked.

'Spirit-animals. Old things. They come from the time before people named them. Some say they are the restless shadows of animals that died in the forests. Some say they are something else entirely. It does not matter what they are. What matters is that you know the rules: sleep on your side, keep your feet from the door, and when they come, do not fight. Let them ride. Let them pass.'

Derek slept on his side for the rest of that visit. He kept his feet from the door. And though he felt the Rounces twice more before he left — the pressure, the weight, the watching — he did not fight, and each time the sensation faded like a tide going out, leaving him whole and breathing in the dark.
moral: Some battles are won not by fighting but by knowing when to yield; the spirits that ride the sleeping are not conquerors but testers of the soul's endurance.

title: Rounce: The Forest Keeper
summary: A timber cutter who defies the old prohibition against felling trees in the deep forest encounters the Rounce, a nature spirit that punishes those who take more than they need and rewards those who leave offerings of respect.
full_text:
In the interior of Saint Vincent, where the volcanic mountains rise so steeply that the clouds snag on their peaks, there is a forest that the old people call the Green Keep. It is dense and ancient and full of sounds that do not belong to birds or wind. The villagers of Fancy and Georgetown have always known about the Green Keep, and they have always known the rule: take what you need, leave an offering, and never cut the great trees that the Rounce has chosen as its own.

Gideon Charles was a timber man who had cut wood in every forest on the island. He was not cruel, but he was practical, and practical men do not believe in spirits that live in trees. When the hurricane of 1987 flattened half the plantations and the demand for building timber doubled, Gideon took his axe into the Green Keep.

He had been there before, at the edges, but never deep. The deeper forest was different. The canopy was so thick that noon was twilight, and the air was cool and wet and smelled of moss and old wood. The trees were enormous — mombin, mahogany, bulletwood — their trunks wider than a man's armspan, their roots crawling over the ground like sleeping serpents.

Gideon marked a tree and swung his axe. The sound was wrong. Instead of the clean ring of steel on wood, there was a thud, as though he had struck something soft. He looked at the blade. It was dull, as though he had been cutting stone. He sharpened it and struck again. The same thud, the same dull blade.

Then the forest went quiet. Not gradually, as a forest quiets at dusk, but all at once, as though a hand had been pressed over every throat. The birds stopped. The insects stopped. Even the wind stopped. And in that silence, Gideon heard breathing that was not his own.

He turned. Standing between two mahogany trees was a figure that was not a figure. It had the shape of a man, but it was made of the forest — bark and vine and fungus and the dark, rich soil of the forest floor. Its eyes were knots in a plank of wood, and its hands were branches, and its voice, when it spoke, was the sound of a tree falling in a place where no one is listening.

'You cut without asking. You take without giving. You do not hear the forest because you have never listened.'

Gideon was not a man who frightened easily, but his legs failed him and he sat down heavily on the root of the tree he had been cutting. 'I meant no harm,' he said, and was surprised to find that it was true.

The Rounce — for that is what the old people would have called it — moved closer. Where it walked, the ground did not dent. It reached out one branch-hand and touched the axe. The steel flaked away like ash.

'The forest gives,' the Rounce said. 'It gives wood and fruit and shade and the breath you are breathing now. It gives without being asked. But the one who takes must also give. A seed. A word. A moment of stillness. You gave nothing. You brought only the axe.'

Gideon understood. He reached into his pocket and took out a handful of seeds — breadfruit seeds he carried to plant in cleared land. He set them on the ground at the base of the tree.

The Rounce looked at the seeds for a long time. Then it stepped back, and the forest sounds returned — tentatively at first, then in a rush, as though a door had been opened.

'Leave,' the Rounce said. 'Take your axe and your seeds and leave. Plant the seeds at the forest's edge. Let the forest grow outward. That is your offering.'

Gideon left the Green Keep that day and never cut timber there again. He planted the seeds at the forest's edge, and they grew into trees that are there still, tall and straight at the border between the wild and the cleared. And when the old people of Fancy tell the story of the Rounce, they tell it with Gideon's name, and they say that the forest keeper is still there, still breathing, still listening for the sound of an axe in a place where no axe should be.
themes: the cost of taking without giving
moral: The forest gives freely, but the one who takes without giving back will face the keeper of what remains; true wealth is not in what you cut but in what you leave standing.

title: Soucouyant: The Fire in the Dark
summary: A young woman who dismisses the old protective rituals of salt and garlic discovers the Soucouyant is real when she sees a ball of fire cross the yard and finds her baby's cribside stained with ash.
full_text:
In the hills above Georgetown, in a house with blue shutters and a zinc roof that sang in the rain, there lived a young mother named Lucille. She had a baby boy, three months old, with eyes like polished river stones and a cry that could wake the dead. Lucille loved him fiercely, but she was modern. She had been to the secondary school. She had read books. She did not believe in Soucouyant.

Her mother, Miss Anise, believed. Miss Anise kept a line of salt across every doorway and hung garlic above the baby's crib. She sprinkled salt on the windowsills and placed a pair of open scissors beneath the baby's mattress. When Lucille asked why, Miss Anise said, 'Because the Soucouyant rides at night, and if she finds a way in, she will feed on the child.'

Lucille smiled and said nothing. She thought the rituals were superstition, the residue of an ignorant age. She let the salt blow away in the wind. She threw out the garlic because it smelled. She removed the scissors because they were a choking hazard.

Three nights after she removed the protections, she woke to a sound. It was not a cry and not a footstep. It was a crackling, like a fire burning in a dry field, and it was coming from outside her window.

She rose and looked out. The yard was silver with moonlight, and there, hovering above the guava tree, was a ball of fire. It was the size of a coconut, bright orange, and it moved with a purpose that fire does not have. It drifted toward the house, leaving a trail of heat that Lucille could feel through the glass.

She froze. Every instinct told her to slam the window shut, but her hands would not obey. The fire-ball paused at the window frame, and for a moment she saw — or imagined she saw — a face within the flame. It was old and sharp and female, with eyes that burned not with light but with hunger.

Then it was gone, slipping through the gap between the window and the frame as though it were smoke.

Lucille ran to the baby's room. He was asleep, his chest rising and falling with the steady rhythm of the innocent. But the crib sheet was warm to the touch, and on the edge of the mattress there was a circle of ash, still faintly smoking, and the smell — acrid, animal, ancient — was the smell of something that should not have been there.

She did not sleep that night. She sat in the chair by the crib, a knife in one hand and a Bible in the other, and she watched the door until dawn.

In the morning, Miss Anise came with fresh salt and new garlic and a bundle of dried herbs that she burned in every room. She did not say I told you so. She simply did what needed to be done, and when it was done, she sat with Lucille on the veranda and drank cocoa tea and said:

'The Soucouyant is not a story for children. She is a woman who learned the old Obeah, the fire-reading, the skin-shedding. By day she is old and harmless. By night she sheds her skin and flies, and she feeds — not to kill, but to take. The blood of the young gives her another year. That is her bargain with whatever darkness she made it with.'

'Is she gone?' Lucille asked.

'She will not come while the salt is down and the garlic hangs. But you must keep the protections. Not because you believe. Because the child is here, and she is out there, and belief has nothing to do with it.'

Lucille kept the protections after that. She salted every doorway herself. She hung the garlic. She placed the scissors beneath the mattress. And on moonlit nights when the air smelled of overripe fruit and old fire, she closed the windows and sat with her baby and did not look outside, because she knew — now, with the certainty of one who has seen — that the ball of fire was real, and it was patient, and it would come again.
moral: The protections of the old ways were not born of ignorance but of knowledge that the modern world has chosen to forget; to discard them is to stand naked before what they held at bay.

title: Haggs: The Twilight Wanderer
summary: A schoolteacher new to the island dismisses the village warnings about the Haggs, a malevolent spirit of the twilight hours, until she finds her classroom filled with the scent of burning herbs and the chalk has written itself on the board.
full_text:
Miss Rowena Clarke arrived in Saint Vincent in the wet season of 1994, sent by the ministry to teach at a small primary school in the village of Troumaca. She was from Kingstown, a city woman, and she regarded the rural villages with a mixture of fondness and pity, the way one regards a relative who still believes in the old ways.

The school was a single building with three classrooms, a rusted flagpole, and a yard that turned to ankle-deep mud when the rains came. The children were bright and quick, and Rowena liked them immediately. But the villagers were reserved in a way that puzzled her. They were polite, even warm, but there were subjects they would not discuss, and one of them was the Haggs.

She first heard the word from an old woman named Miss Priscilla, who swept the schoolyard each morning. 'You must not stay after dark,' Miss Priscilla said, her broom beating the ground with emphasis. 'The Haggs comes at twilight. It walks the roads and the schoolyard and the churchyard. It brings bad luck to those who see it, and worse luck to those who do not look away.'

Rowena thanked her and thought nothing more of it. She was a woman of education and reason, and she did not believe in spirits that walked at twilight.

But the warnings continued. The headmaster, Mr. Charles, asked her politely to lock the classroom by six. The parents of her students asked if she could arrange dismissal before the evening bell. Even the children whispered about the Haggs, though they fell silent whenever she asked them what they meant.

One evening in late October, Rowena stayed late to grade papers. The classroom was small and hot, and the ceiling fan made a sound like a slow heartbeat. She worked by the light of a single bulb, and when she looked up, the sky outside the window had turned the colour of a bruise — purple and grey and deepening toward black.

She gathered her papers and stood to leave. Then the light flickered. It did not go out; it wavered, as though something had passed between the bulb and the room, and in that moment the air changed. It grew cool and heavy, and with it came a smell — thick, herbal, like sage and smoke and something older, something that had no name in Rowena's vocabulary.

The chalk on the blackboard moved. She watched it — actually watched it — as a word appeared in her own handwriting, or a close imitation of it: LEAVE.

Rowena did not leave. She stood very still and looked at the word and felt, for the first time in her adult life, a fear that was not of the dark or of the unknown but of the certainty that something was in the room with her and that it was not human. It was not an animal. It was a presence, a weight in the air, a wrongness that pressed against her thoughts and made them scatter like chickens in a rain.

She picked up the chalk and wrote beneath the first word: WHO ARE YOU?

The answer appeared instantly, the letters jagged and sharp: HAGGS.

Then the light steadied, the smell faded, and the room was empty. Rowena stood there for a long time, her hands shaking, her papers on the floor. When she finally locked the door and walked home, the twilight was over and the stars were out, and she did not look at the shadows between the houses.

She never stayed late again. She locked the classroom by five-thirty and walked home with the other teachers, and when Miss Priscilla told her stories about the Haggs — how it came on Hop-tu-Naa nights and festival eves, how it brought misfortune and madness to those who provoked it — Rowena listened. She did not argue. She did not explain. She had seen the word on the board, and she knew that some things do not require belief to be real.

Years later, when she had become one of the old teachers that the new ones came to for advice, she would tell them the same thing Miss Priscilla had told her: do not stay after dark, do not walk the roads at twilight, and if the chalk writes on the board by itself, do not answer it. Leave. Lock the door. Come back in the morning, when the Haggs has gone back to wherever the Haggs goes when the sun is high.
moral: Knowledge of the world comes not only from books but from the places where books have not yet gone; to dismiss the warnings of those who have seen what you have not is not wisdom but arrogance.
